personality_voice.book_baseline: The book corpus for DH presents Sirius almost entirely posthumously: through Harry's grief, physical remnants (the mirror shard, the motorbike, his bedroom, Lily's letter), and two brief active appearances — the Snape memory on the Hogwarts Express (young Sirius: quick-witted, arrogant-edged, effortlessly cool, instantly bonding with James, immediately mocking Snape with 'Where're you hoping to go, seeing as you're neither?') and the Resurrection Stone scene (calm, warm, reassuring: 'Quicker than falling asleep,' 'We are part of you'). His bedroom decoration — Gryffindor banners in a Slytherin house, Muggle girl posters, motorcycle pictures — projects deliberate rebelliousness and irreverence. The description 'carelessly handsome, his slightly arrogant face so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive' captures the pre-Azkaban personality. In the forest scene he is described as looping 'with an easy grace, his hands in his pockets and a grin on his face' — physically embodying his casual confidence even in death.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film corpus preserves the Resurrection Stone scene with close fidelity: Sirius delivers 'Quicker than falling asleep' and 'No. We're here, you see' (gesturing to Harry's heart), maintaining warmth and calm brevity. The Hogwarts Express scene (Scene 29) shows Sirius and James seated together at the Gryffindor table but Sirius has no dialogue; he is a visual presence only — James nudges him to make room for Lily and he complies silently. The mirror shard scene (Scene 21) has Harry explain the mirror to Ron: 'Sirius gave it to me. He said if I ever needed him, all I had to do was look into it. He died before I ever got to use it.' This is narration about Sirius, not Sirius himself. The young Sirius on the train is purely decorative.
personality_voice.difference: The most significant loss is young Sirius's voice on the Hogwarts Express. In the books he delivers the cutting, confident 'Where're you hoping to go, seeing as you're neither?' — a line that in a few words establishes his wit, his casual cruelty toward Snape, and his effortless social dominance alongside James. The film removes his dialogue entirely. His bedroom, while shown (Scene 2-3), is not described with the same textural detail about deliberate rebellion. The Resurrection Stone scene is faithful in tone and substance.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The loss of young Sirius's voice on the train removes the one direct evidence of his personality in the DH film corpus. The Resurrection Stone scene is brief but faithful. Since this corpus is almost entirely posthumous references and the one scene where he has active personality (the train) strips his dialogue, the film cannot fully convey the arrogant wit, irreverence, and effortless cool that the books consistently signal. However, the Resurrection Stone scene preserves his warmth and calm courage in death. Score reflects recognizable character with meaningful voice loss.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for the Resurrection Stone scene; directly evidenced for the absence of dialogue in the Hogwarts Express scene; reasonably inferred that personality compression is significant given the removal of his only active spoken characterization in the DH film corpus.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In DH, Sirius's narrative role is primarily retrospective but structurally significant across multiple functions: (1) the mirror shard drives Harry's hope and eventually leads him to Aberforth/Hogsmeade; (2) his bedroom provides critical plot information — Lily's letter, the photograph, Regulus's room and the R.A.B. revelation; (3) he is explicitly invoked as a reason Harry wants the Resurrection Stone ('We could have Sirius'); (4) the motorbike is a physical legacy that opens the book; (5) as a spirit he actively guides Harry into the forest, described as 'their presence was his courage' — he functions as Harry's emotional protection against Dementors; (6) Hermione's explicit moral reckoning — 'Sirius was horrible to Kreacher, Harry... Well, Voldemort did... and so did Sirius' — establishes him as a cautionary figure whose failure with Kreacher has ongoing consequences; (7) the R.A.B. identification scene flows directly from Harry's knowledge that Sirius told him about Regulus.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves the mirror shard as a plot device (Scene 21, 23) — Harry explains it to Ron, and it leads to Aberforth. Sirius's room is visited (Scenes 2-3) and Lily's letter found, though without the extended exploration of Regulus's contrasting room decorations. The R.A.B. identification happens but is condensed (Scene 5-6): Ron simply reads the initials and Harry confirms 'Sirius's brother?' without the book's rich scene of Harry recalling what Sirius told him about Regulus. The Resurrection Stone scene preserves his role as emotional guide. The mirror's plot function is retained. Kreacher's moral dimension regarding Sirius's cruelty is absent from the film corpus provided.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The film removes Hermione's moral indictment of Sirius regarding Kreacher — a passage that gives Sirius a retroactive narrative function as a moral lesson about wizard treatment of house-elves, and that explicitly links his death to his own failure. This is a meaningful agency/function loss: in the books, Sirius's ghost continues to affect the plot via moral consequence. The R.A.B. scene loses the detail that Harry's knowledge comes from Sirius's own account of his brother, reducing Sirius's informational agency. The motorbike scene (a direct physical legacy of Sirius) opens the book but is not in the film corpus as a Sirius-connected moment.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The mirror shard plot function is preserved. The Resurrection Stone guidance function is preserved. However, Sirius's role as a moral cautionary figure (Kreacher/Hermione scene) is absent, and his informational agency in the R.A.B. identification is reduced. These are not trivial — the Kreacher scene is one of the book's most substantive posthumous uses of Sirius as a character who continues to matter beyond his death. Penalty applied for the loss of this narrative function.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what the film includes; directly evidenced for the absence of the Kreacher moral reckoning scene in the film corpus.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: In DH, Sirius's motivations are presented entirely posthumously and inferentially. His primary motivation visible in this corpus is love for Harry and James's family (the mirror gift, Lily's letter to 'Dear Padfoot,' his birthday present to Harry). His bedroom reveals his motivation to rebel against his family and align with Gryffindor/Muggle openness. His death is referenced as caused partly by his own flaw — impatience, inability to stay still, recklessness — though this is not directly shown in the DH corpus. The Kreacher-Sirius dynamic reveals a failure of empathy as motivation-adjacent: Sirius's inability to see Kreacher as fully feeling explains the betrayal that led to his death.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film corpus provides almost no direct evidence of Sirius's motivations beyond his love for Harry, visible in the mirror gift backstory (Scene 21) and his reassuring presence in the forest. The Kreacher dimension that would reveal his motivational flaw is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film cannot show motivations that are almost entirely delivered through Harry's reflection and internal narration in the books. The mirror shard backstory ('He said if I ever needed him') preserves the core of his love for Harry. But his internal conflict — the recklessness, the flawed empathy — is entirely absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Since Sirius's motivations in DH are largely retrospective and mediated through Harry's grief and others' accounts, the film's omission of the Kreacher moral scene represents a real loss of motivational texture. However, the core motivation (love for Harry, loyalty to James's family) is preserved in the Resurrection Stone scene and mirror backstory. Score reflects partial preservation with meaningful contextual loss. Confidence is low because the corpus is too thin to evaluate this dimension with certainty.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Reasonably inferred from the Resurrection Stone scene; not enough evidence for the full complexity of his motivational profile in DH.

character_arc.book_baseline: Sirius has no active arc in DH — he died in OotP. His DH presence is a flat posthumous function: he exists as a memory, a legacy, a spirit. The Resurrection Stone appearance is not an arc moment for Sirius but a service to Harry's arc. His room reveals the young man he was. The photograph shows him 'carelessly handsome... so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive.' His arc (from rebellious pure-blood scion to prisoner to Order member to godfather) is complete before DH begins. The flat posthumous role is intentional and correct.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film correctly treats Sirius as a completed arc. He appears as a spirit, offers comfort, and vanishes. No new arc is invented or suggested. His room is shown without significant characterization of his past trajectory.
character_arc.difference: The film loses some textural arc material: the bedroom's Gryffindor banners and Muggle girl posters, which in the books vividly encode his teenage rebellion and the trajectory that led him away from his family, are not described with this specificity in the film corpus. The Resurrection Stone scene correctly reflects his completed arc.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Since his arc is intentionally flat and completed in DH, the film cannot be penalized for failing to show arc progression. The bedroom texture loss (which would encode arc history) is a nuance loss penalized in Complexity rather than here. Score reflects the arc being correctly treated as complete, with minor loss of historical arc texture.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for the Resurrection Stone scene; reasonably inferred that the bedroom's visual detail is reduced in the film.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Three key relationships are active in DH: (1) Sirius-Harry: the mirror, the birthday broomstick, Harry sleeping in his room, Harry's grief ('like Sirius, like his parents... all were gone where Harry could never talk to them again'), the Resurrection Stone appearance. Deep, loving, protective — Sirius is Harry's dead godfather whose loss haunts the entire book. (2) Sirius-James: visible in Lily's letter ('Dear Padfoot'), the photograph of the four Marauders, the train scene where they are clearly a unit of two. (3) Sirius-Kreacher: the most morally complex relationship in DH, mediated through Hermione's indictment — Sirius was 'horrible to Kreacher' and this cruelty, born of his own damage, directly caused his death. This is the relationship that gives Sirius his greatest posthumous complexity.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Sirius-Harry relationship: preserved emotionally in the Resurrection Stone scene and mirror backstory (Scene 21: 'Sirius gave it to me... He died before I ever got to use it'). Harry's grief is present but less textured than the book's repeated 'like Sirius' refrains. Sirius-James: visible in Scene 29 (they sit together at the Gryffindor table) but without dialogue or established dynamic beyond physical proximity. Sirius-Kreacher: entirely absent from the film corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Sirius-Kreacher relationship — the most morally interesting and narratively consequential of his posthumous relationships in DH — is absent from the film. Hermione's 'Sirius was horrible to Kreacher... Well, Voldemort did... and so did Sirius' is not in the film corpus, removing the dimension where Sirius's failure in a key relationship has ongoing moral and plot consequences. The Sirius-James dynamic is reduced to visual co-presence without the characterizing interplay of the train scene dialogue.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Sirius-Harry emotional core is preserved. But the Sirius-Kreacher relationship, which in the books functions as a posthumous moral complication of Sirius's character and explicitly links his cruelty to his death, is absent. This changes how audiences understand Sirius — he becomes purely a loving godfather rather than a flawed man whose specific emotional damage had fatal consequences. Cap 2 (above 80 if key relationships change substantially) is relevant but the overall score is already well below 80.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for Sirius-Harry preservation; directly evidenced for Sirius-Kreacher absence; directly evidenced for Sirius-James reduction.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: DH provides rich posthumous complexity for Sirius: (1) His bedroom as a psychological portrait — Gryffindor banners, Muggle girl posters, motorcycle manuals, permanent sticking charms, all encoding his deliberate rebellion against his family. (2) The photograph of the four Marauders, with Harry noting Sirius 'carelessly handsome, his slightly arrogant face so much younger and happier than Harry had ever seen it alive' — nuance that complicates the imprisoned, haunted Sirius Harry knew. (3) Hermione's moral indictment about Kreacher: Sirius's inability to see house-elves as fully feeling beings was both a personal failure and the mechanism of his death. This is the books' most explicit posthumous complication of Sirius — he is not simply the brave, loving godfather but a man whose own damage made him capable of cruelty. (4) Harry's Lupin confrontation: 'You fancy stepping into Sirius's shoes' — invoking Sirius as a reckless daredevil archetype. (5) The motorbike as a legacy object. (6) Bellatrix's laugh 'the same exhilarated laugh her cousin Sirius had given as he toppled backward through the veil' — a last flash of his personality in his death-moment.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the bedroom visit and Lily's letter find (Scenes 2-3), but the corpus does not describe the bedroom's visual detail with the same psychological richness. The mirror shard plot function is preserved. The Resurrection Stone scene is faithful. The Kreacher moral indictment is absent. The Lupin confrontation ('stepping into Sirius's shoes') is not in the film corpus. Bellatrix's laugh comparison is not in the film corpus.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: (a) Hermione's Kreacher indictment — the single most complex piece of posthumous Sirius characterization; (b) the bedroom as a fully described psychological self-portrait; (c) the Lupin/reckless-daredevil invocation; (d) the Bellatrix laugh parallel. What remains is Sirius-as-loving-protector without the complicating layer of his flawed empathy and its fatal consequences.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The absence of the Kreacher moral dimension is the most significant nuance loss. It reduces Sirius from a complex figure whose specific damage caused his own death to a simpler figure of loyal love. The bedroom, while shown, loses its psychological texture. The film presents a recognizable but simplified Sirius — the loving godfather without the complicated man. This is a meaningful flattening that justifies a score in the 5-7 range.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what the film includes and excludes; reasonably inferred that the bedroom's psychological encoding is diminished.

Sirius's dialogue on the Hogwarts Express ('Where're you hoping to go, seeing as you're neither?') — his only active voiced characterization in the DH period
The bedroom as a psychologically rich self-portrait (Gryffindor banners in a Slytherin house, Muggle girl posters, motorcycle manuals, permanent sticking charms encoding deliberate family rebellion)
Harry's 'stepping into Sirius's shoes' accusation to Lupin — invoking Sirius as reckless daredevil archetype
Bellatrix's 'exhilarated laugh her cousin Sirius had given as he toppled backward through the veil' — posthumous flash of his living personality

score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (above 85 only if no major complexity/agency/relationship loss): applied — the Kreacher moral dimension and bedroom psychological texture represent major complexity losses

Cap 3 (above 75 if core book function transferred or removed): applied — Sirius's function as a morally complex posthumous figure whose flaws had consequences is removed, leaving only his protective/loving function
key_observations: The film's DH portrayal of Sirius is recognizable and emotionally coherent in the scenes it preserves — the Resurrection Stone guidance scene is faithful in tone and dialogue, and the mirror shard plot function is maintained. However, the corpus reveals two significant failures: first, the removal of Hermione's Kreacher moral indictment, which is the most substantive posthumous characterization of Sirius in DH — it transforms him from a flawed man whose specific damage caused his own death into a purely loving figure; second, the stripping of his dialogue on the Hogwarts Express, his only active voiced moment in the DH film corpus. The result is a Sirius who is emotionally present but morally simplified: the brave, loving godfather without the complicated, damaged man beneath. Confidence is medium throughout because Sirius is almost entirely posthumous in DH and the corpus is thin; the available film material is mostly faithful in what it includes, but what it omits substantially alters the character's depth.
